finding.claim: The DELETE /projects/:id handler calls authorized(), which returns a boolean, but ignores the result. Any authenticated user can delete any project they don't own.
finding.source: Authenticated non-owner, non-admin user sends DELETE /projects/<victim project id>. The id comes from req.params.id.

trace.note: Project loaded by request id with no ownership check
authorized(req.user, project) returns false for a non-owner, but the return value is discarded. There is no if, return or throw.
authorized() only returns a boolean. Unlike authorize() at line 4, it never throws.

finding.guards_checked: authorize() throws, but this route calls the non-throwing authorized(). No router-level middleware is visible in the file, and the router has no auth guard of its own. req.user is assumed to be populated upstream. Even if so, there is no ownership enforcement here.

verdict.guard_found: authorized() at api.js:12-14 (returns a boolean, never throws) is called as a bare statement at api.js:18, so it has no effect; authorize() at api.js:4 throws but is only used in the PUT route (api.js:25). No router-level middleware exists in api.js, and it is the only file in the directory.
verdict.reason: api.js:18 calls the boolean-returning authorized() and discards the result, so api.js:19 deletes the project for any authenticated non-owner, unlike the PUT route at api.js:25, which correctly uses the throwing authorize().

finding.claim: PUT /projects/:id/name stores req.body.name with no type or length validation, and the project object is returned as-is. This is a low-impact issue. The authorize() check is correct, so it is not an authorization bypass. Low confidence, probably not exploitable beyond the owner's own data.
finding.source: Project owner or admin, via req.body.name.

trace.note: The name is assigned without validation

finding.guards_checked: Ownership is enforced by authorize(). If a project is missing, projects.get may return undefined, which would cause a TypeError and a 500. That is only a robustness issue.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at api.js:4-10 throws a 403 error when the user is neither the owner nor an admin. It is called as a bare statement at api.js:25, which is correct because it throws rather than returning a value.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate (api.js:25 authorize throws, api.js:26 assigns the name unvalidated), but only the owner or an admin can reach api.js:26, and they already have the power to rename the project, so missing validation there is not a vulnerability. Separately, the DELETE route at api.js:18 discards the result of authorized() and so has a real authorization bypass, but that is a different finding.
